deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no words or formulas. It is a sheet of colour sketches drawn on the back of a CRAY2 line-printer banner (JOB 344, 19 AUG 82). In the context of cote 154, the sketches explore how to draw arrangements of pseudo-lines in the real projective plane P^2(R), using several topological models.

(1) Disc model. The disc stands for P^2 with antipodal boundary points identified. Pseudo-lines are orange arcs ending at pairs of (roughly) antipodal boundary points. One such disc is at left-middle, and the large disc at centre has a thick 'line at infinity' drawn across it.

(2) Hemisphere / sphere model. Several half-discs and spheres are drawn with a dark-green rim and a dashed green or blue-grey equator. This is P^2 seen as the sphere modulo the antipodal map, with pseudo-lines lifted to pseudo-great-circles drawn in perspective on the upper hemisphere. The bottom-centre empty green half-disc with a dashed upper rim is a blank template of this view. The tall oval at top centre appears to show a circle (sphere with dashed equator) nested in a larger closed curve. A plausible reading is a double-cover or 'two hemispheres' picture, with pseudo-lines continuing from one cap to the other.

(3) Rectangle / strip model. The square at top right and the rounded rectangle at middle right can be read as a Möbius band, i.e. P^2 minus a point, with the vertical sides identified after a twist. Pseudo-lines become wavy curves crossing the strip, and a dashed inner rectangle marks a sub-region.

(4) Periodic strip (top centre). Wavy orange curves run across a band divided by vertical lines. Dark-green and blue-grey brackets mark one fundamental domain of a periodic pattern. The triangular cells between curve crossings are shaded orange. This matches the representation of an arrangement as a periodic wiring diagram on the universal cover of the Möbius band, with attention to the triangular faces. Levi's theorem says that a simple arrangement of n pseudo-lines has at least n triangles.

(5) Straight-line configurations (left). Two green pencils of three lines each, through two points joined by a vertical segment, plus some orange/brown lines crossing a green horizontal line. These are the stretchable, straight-line reference configurations. A faint pencil curvilinear triangle and a faint pencil 'cylinder/handle' outline are also present.

The page serves the general programme of cote 154: understanding combinatorial types of pseudo-line systems in P^2 and their various drawings. Read alongside the next page, which carries a cell complex with a blue dual graph, it also serves cell decompositions and their duals.

ideas.modern_name: wiring diagrams / allowable sequences on the Möbius band; Levi's triangle lemma (at least n triangles)

ideas.modern_name: Möbius strip model of the projective plane

deep.surprise_reason: These are purely exploratory drawings of pseudo-line arrangements in standard models of P^2: disc, hemisphere, Möbius strip, periodic wiring diagram. There is no text, claim or construction beyond what is classical (Levi, Ringel, Grünbaum, Goodman–Pollack). They are of documentary interest only, showing Grothendieck's visual working method.
transcription_corrections: Top left: two green pencils of three straight lines each, through two points on a common vertical segment, with a faint pencil curved figure behind them. These are straight-line configurations rather than pseudo-line drawings.

Top centre: a rectangle divided by vertical lines with wavy orange curves forming a periodic pattern. Triangular cells are shaded orange, and a fundamental domain is bracketed in dark green and blue-grey, suggesting a periodic wiring-diagram picture.
Top middle: a tall green oval enclosing a circle with a dashed blue-grey equator, crossed by orange pseudo-lines. Possibly a sphere or double-cover picture.
Bottom centre: an empty green half-disc with a dashed upper rim (hemisphere template), next to a faint pencil outline of a vertical 'cylinder/handle' shape.
Centre: a faint pencil curvilinear triangle (three concave sides).
The '100' at bottom left is the archive page number (it appears mirrored in the image).
